articles.title: Your coding agent is privileged automation: a workstation baseline for Claude Code
articles.excerpt: A coding agent reads the repository, runs shell commands with the developer's privileges, edits code and calls external tools. On the workstation, the least production-like place it runs, it is often…
articles.body: A coding agent reads the repository, runs shell commands with the developer's privileges, edits code and calls external tools. On the workstation, the least production-like place it runs, it is often left ungoverned. But distance from production does not remove the path to production. This is a condensed version of a baseline from the AI Delivery Factory reference, written for a regulated firm running Claude Code on managed Windows with WSL2, Linux workstations and hosted CI. It is vendor-specific on purpose. The settings file is not the boundary Managed settings are a client-side control, not a security boundary. A local administrator can edit the managed source, and managed settings bind only Claude Code. Every high-risk context needs an OS or network control behind the policy file.

articles.title: Python | Looping Problems
articles.excerpt: 1. Chocolate Wrapper Problem Problem You have Rs. 100 /- One chocolate costs Rs. 5. Every time you buy a chocolate, you get one wrapper. You can exchange 3 wrappers for 1 additional chocolate. What is…
articles.body: 1. Chocolate Wrapper Problem Problem You have Rs. 100 /- One chocolate costs Rs. 5. Every time you buy a chocolate, you get one wrapper. You can exchange 3 wrappers for 1 additional chocolate. What is the maximum number of chocolates you can have with Rs. 100? Flowchart See the first flowchart below. Algorithm Set the total money as 100. Set the chocolate price as 5. Calculate the number of chocolates we can buy. Store the number of chocolates in a variable called total_chocolates . Store the same number in wrappers , because each chocolate gives one wrapper. Use a while loop to check whether we have at least 3 wrappers. If the condition is true: Exchange 3 wrappers for 1 chocolate. Add 1 to the total chocolates. Add the new chocolate's wrapper.

articles.title: Deterministic PR Gates for Agent-Generated Code: How to Reject Fixes That Can't Prove Themselves
articles.excerpt: AI agents now open 17 million pull requests per month. Most of them claim to fix bugs. Some of them do. Many look plausible but break existing tests, weaken coverage, or solve the wrong problem. The g…
articles.body: AI agents now open 17 million pull requests per month. Most of them claim to fix bugs. Some of them do. Many look plausible but break existing tests, weaken coverage, or solve the wrong problem. The gap between "I fixed it" and "here is proof" is where human review time burns. Sarvar Nadaf built a deterministic Python gate that sits between agent commit and human review. It checks evidence, not promises. No LLM grades the LLM. The gate runs against Amazon Nova Pro agent output and posts rejection reasons directly to the PR when proof is missing. The Problem: Claims Without Evidence An agent reads a GitHub issue, generates a fix, opens a PR, and writes "done, one fix." A human reviewer sees green CI and assumes the agent did what it said.

articles.title: The 1/20-cost model scored less than half the coding points — so I made the 60-second proof public
articles.excerpt: I've been running a small eval harness that pits a budget model against a frontier one on the same fixed set of coding tasks. The result kept surprising me: the cheap model runs at roughly 1/20 the pe…
articles.body: I've been running a small eval harness that pits a budget model against a frontier one on the same fixed set of coding tasks. The result kept surprising me: the cheap model runs at roughly 1/20 the per-token cost and lands well under half the coding score of the big one. Numbers on a spreadsheet don't convince anyone, so I recorded the whole run as a short walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Kk0DbwAPBTU Here's the concrete detail of how it works. The harness feeds each task to both models with identical prompts and temperature 0, then scores pass@1 against a held-out test set — no retries, no cherry-picking. Cost is computed from the provider's published per-token rates times actual completion tokens, so a verbose model pays for its own verbosity.

articles.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
articles.excerpt: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
articles.body: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Here's how it helped Apollo astronauts.
articles.body: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 .

articles.title: NICER Status Updates
articles.excerpt: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explor…
articles.body: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.  The mission and space station teams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array. In June 2025, NICER was suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects. The team paused data collection to investigate the issue.
